utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Morning, sir. Would you -- the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies today, of course, and Mr. Popovic is continuing his questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, General, sir. We will continue where we left off yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at document D011-1274, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In your binder this is tab 15. The number is D011-1274.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at page 2 in both versions, this is 1275, and can we look at the following page in both versions, please. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we've seen that on the previous pages you're stating what the situation is in the 1st and 2nd Army, then we look at 2.3 where you're talking about the 3rd Army. And then in the first paragraph you're saying: "It was assessed that the volume and complexity of the tasks faced by military judicial organs in this strategic group was too great a load for the existing establishment, and after making adjustments and overcoming initial difficulties the military judicial organs have become fully operational." Can you please tell us the following: The 3rd Army, exactly which army is this, and can you please give us your comments on this paragraph that we have just read?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Army is the Nis Army which had its unit in the Kosovo and Metohija area as well as courts that were distributed in the area of that army. They were covering the Kosovo and Metohija associated territory. Yesterday when I was talking about the numbers of judges per establishment, this was actually something that was put down on paper. But the actual number of judges that were out in the field was insufficient. So the number of judges and prosecutors was increased, particularly in the Pristina Corps, so professional and other technical staff for logistics and security were added. So this is the assessment and the note after completing this task, because I made this information after I toured all the courts and on the basis of all the suggestions made previously, suggesting that these establishment and logistical questions had to be resolved in the best possible manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: The same paragraph, item 2 says: "The first-instance organs attached to the command of the 3rd Army, the Nis Corps and the Nis Military District, have proved extremely efficient, unlike the judicial organs attached to the command of the military district in Nis." When one reads this paragraph we can see that the logic is not quite right. I assume this is a slip or a mistake. So could you please clarify what would need to be corrected in order for this to make sense because the Nis military district is mentioned twice.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a typographical error in the last sentence because this is the command of the military district in Pristina, actually, that is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I would like to move to paragraph 3 of this same section, which states: "Military judicial organs attached to the Pristina Corps command have encountered in their work very complex criminal cases and then -- that deal with serious crimes (terrorism, murder, robbery, theft) which require the prosecutors and judges to have a high degree of expertise and experience." Could you please clarify this position, primarily the fact that the offences the judicial organs were deal with in that area also include terrorism, and also what would be the competence to try acts of terrorism of the -- of those organs and in what manner could this be prosecuted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary of the situation, global situation. At that time it was already noticed - this was in May - that there were a lot of serious complex crimes in that area with a number of perpetrators. So the military courts were authorised to act for all offences committed by members of that unit on the one hand, and on the other hand --- there was the KLA on the other hand. So these crimes were numbered according to the gravity. These are acts committed by illegal Albanian armed formations because the whole time they used the terrorist method of fighting, which is very serious, unpredictable, can crop up anywhere. Already at that time we did have several raids on military facilities and members of the army. A number of times, even at the time, what happened actually on three occasions witnesses who would come to the tribunal were intercepted on their way back to their units, and they actually never came back and their fate has not been discovered until this day. So this is an issue that deserves analysis in any case. Then we have killings, robberies, with serious consequences. We did have such cases too. This did occur more and more and this was noted in the report, so it was already reaching the prosecutor and the court. We are talking only about these types of crimes and the forms that they appeared in, the way that was presented to the court and the prosecutor and the information that the prosecutors had submitted to the courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We said that this document was drafted on the 12th of May. From the time the state of war was declared some time had passed. Was it only now possible to draw conclusions, and were you only at that time able to compile documents and information from all the courts in order to be able to make any kind of summary as you did here?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's logical that from the beginning of the aggression, from the time the state of war was declared, the courts were not able to proceed with cases immediately. This is one thing. Secondly, from the time an offence was committed to the time that it was processed some time had passed, reports were submitted, investigations were initiated, there was detention, a period of that, and then the court would take up the case. So that took up some time. This was of a processing nature, and then this analysis was made after I visited all of those courts. So this situation was already noted then, which needed to be assessed and pointed out.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask to look at the following pages in the B/C/S and English versions of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'm going to ask you to look at item 3 or section 3, which is titled: "Number of Cases." And you have just talked to us about information that you received from the military judicial organs, and so in this section 3 you cite the number of criminal reports, file requests for the investigations, charges, sentences, persons accused. Could you please tell us what this information is and what is the source of the information that you quoted in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The speakers are kindly asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This section when we analyse it and we see that the number of the perpetrators of crimes has increased, this of course had to be documented with certain data. Data was received directly from the military prosecutor and from the courts when I went to visit those places, and the supreme military court and supreme military prosecutor monitored the situation daily in their organisational entities. And here it is shown where it says that until then the prosecutor received 7.800 -- 7.807 criminal reports and submitted requests for investigations. It's not shown whether they actually submitted requests to submitted charges.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He submitted 2.911 requests for the investigation, and charged 3.897 persons. There's probably an error in the numbers here. This is seen in the following sentence. So 3.897 criminal charges were submitted or indictments were issued against such number of persons, and at that time the basic, lower courts pronounced 997 judgements.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And we have this number here ending with 2.393 criminal cases. So this takes it to account the investigations completed and the cases completed, so then you have the total number of cases completed by the courts from their area of jurisdiction. So this indicates a fairly efficient manner of working in such a short period of time, and we all well know that the legal procedure must be ensured even in conditions of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In order to avoid confusion about this number, about completed 2.393 criminal cases, yesterday you explained the investigating procedure conducted pursuant to the Law on Criminal Procedure in the Republic of Serbia and the FRY. Does this number of 2.393 cases include completed investigations by the court, following which the prosecutor is able to issue an indictment and further process the case?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The investigating judge, when he completes the investigation, hands over the case to the prosecutor; and at that point in time, as far as he's concerned, the case is completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It still then remains up to the prosecutor to continue the case before the court, so this does not mean that the whole case is absolutely finished but only that the investigative part conducted by the court has been completed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And the number of 997 judgements means that judgements were passed and the first-instance proceedings was completed before the military court?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at section 4: "Basic Problems."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And we're going to look at paragraph 2 where it says: "There is a slight increase in more complex crime, with an increasing number of perpetrators committing serious crimes, which represents a threat to society and requires the greater engagement of competent organs in order to uncover and prevent the same." Before I asked you to comment on this particular paragraph, this sentence "there is a slight increase in more complex crimes." Can you please clarify what was meant with the term "complex, more complex crimes." Once again, there is insistence on uncovering and preventing crimes, so I would like your comments on that point as well.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we're talking about this evaluation or assessment, more complex crimes, what we're primarily talking about are serious, grave crimes in which there are a number of perpetrators. The manner of commission is such that it is very difficult to uncover such a crime and prove it. So in that sense it is complex. Any case which by its nature -- and the consequences of a particular criminal act results in their complexity. As far as prosecuting such a crime is concerned, we have information that has already reached the prosecutor, criminal reports, information from those criminal reports, and information acquired by the court. In the previous paragraph we forgot to indicate these 205 on-site investigations conducted by the investigating judge. The investigating judge, as he's obliged to do by law, went to a scene of a crime. Once a prosecutor is informed about a crime being committed, then the investigating judge is obliged, if the security situation permits, to go to the scene of the crime and to conduct an on-site investigation and make a report on that. All such investigation by the investigating judge contain his assessment of exactly what happened, how the crime was committed. So then we have this occurrence of a more complex crime occurring with a number of perpetrators, and this makes our work more difficult for the prosecutor and the police investigation organs. So that is why this assessment is given here, that assessments need to be made; this is sent to the units and unit commands that they need to take measures of prevention to prevent such crimes. And if the crimes are committed, then they need to take measures to have these crimes uncovered as soon as possible, because wherever you have these complex crimes with several perpetrators, these usually isolated groups of individuals, it's very difficult to uncover such crimes because you don't have senior officers everywhere and there are no organs monitoring this everywhere in order to be able to uncover a serious crime. You would only find out about that indirectly and then retroactively you are trying to obtain this legally valid evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now move to the following page in the B/C/S and the English versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, please take a look at item 6, sub-item 3. The heading is, Lower levels, and under 1 it says: "All uniformed officers must immediately report to the competent military prosecutor any crime and their perpetrators so that they can be prosecuted, and any officer who do not adhere to this will be made accountable and the strictest measures will be applied against them." Again, I'm going to ask you to comment this paragraph and to explain to us whether this continued insistence on detection, reporting of the perpetrators, and the duties of officers, whether this was done.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the permanent attitude of the staff of the Supreme Command. This is what we kept insisting on. This is a permanent task on the one hand; on the other hand, it is my -- me, in my capacity as head of the legal administration and not as a private individual insisted on that. And it could be seen that wherever problems were identified and analysed - and after all this chapter 6 is proposed measures, which means that whenever a problem is identified I proposed measures to be undertaken, both to prevent such occurrences on the one hand, and on the other hand where certain things had happened to propose measures to undertake to make sure that everybody take action within their remit to remedy the situation. You see the different levels tasks for the Supreme Command Staff, for strategic group staff, for units and organs at other level and those list of steps to be done by everybody who would uncover criminal offences. In 80 to 90 per cent of cases they did so, and there can be no major objection to their conduct. So 80 to 90 per cent of the crimes that did happen there was reported and detected by the lower-level units' officers. Of course they couldn't do everything under the circumstances, and we continued appealing -- not just appealing, ordering them to report crimes. And in cases where somebody knew of criminal offences and failed to report, then appropriate legal action should be taken against such person because it is the duty of all military personnel, officers and soldiers, to do so, particularly in cases of criminal offences against the health, lives of persons, civilians, prisoners of war, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I move to tender this into document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 12th of May, I'm -- 12th of May, 1999. This is what we established at the very beginning, since there was a mistake in the translation into English. There was an annotation of 12th of September, 1999, in the upper right-hand corner, but I asked the witness about that, and he confirmed the 12th of May, 1999, as being the right date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00506.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's see D011-1263.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, that would be tab 14 in your binder. As you can see, this is a table entitled: "List of Convictions Per Category of Person, Type of Criminal Offence, and Length of Sentences as of on the 15th of May, 1999." First of all, given that we've seen the document just now was dated the 12th of May, 1999, is there any connection between the previous document and this list and this table? And after that, please, explain to us the method of drawing up this table and what it indicates.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are several other tables which supported the information dated the 12th of May. The information was drafted on the 12th of May, 1999. After a couple of days these specific figures were collated and sent on the 15th of May together with the information that we just saw because there is an indication that there are tables as annexes to that document. These tables contain the date the 15th of May because this is when we got the information and the figures from the supreme military court and the supreme prosecutor on the number of cases. You see the number of convictions by type of crime and by sentence as handed down by first-instance courts. And this is what is displayed here, to provide a specific overview of the number of cases either pending or completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we take a look at this list, we see that there are certain types of criminal offences in certain columns together with figures. Before we go through the criminal offences listed here, could you please tell us which article of the penal code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the penal code of the Republic of Serbia or articles which were invoked by military prosecutors concerning violations of international humanitarian law during the state of war in Kosovo in 1999.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: See, there are criminal offences against the body and life, murder, woundings, grave bodily harm. These are under the heading of criminal offences against body and life, and -- or life and limb, and by -- they're categorised by victim and the manner of perpetration. And some of them are criminal offences violating international humanitarian law in the state of war. This would be one and the same thing, but prosecutors used the legal qualification of such criminal offence as a criminal offence of murder because in the republican law this is a capital offence, which means punishable by capital punishment, whereas in the federal legislation there was no capital punishment, and this is why they used this more grave qualification and -- but this was changed in -- later on and more lenient legal qualification was used.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's make this matter easier to understand. What was the criminal offence that you were discussing? Is it Article 47 of the Serbian penal code, that would be murder?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's Article 47, murder under the Serbian penal code, which are punishable by death sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That includes murder of multiple victims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, multiple victims under difficult circumstances, as prevailed in Kosovo and Metohija; and particularly if there were multiple co-perpetrators, and that qualification included murder of two or more persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the penalty for that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The alternative penalty was capital punishment or custodial sentence of 15 years of prison or more --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I intervene, Mr. Popovic. Are you saying, sir, that the offences in the category crimes against life and limb were offences of murder, or did they merely include the possibility of offences of murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a chapter in the penal code entitled: "Crimes Against Life and Limb," including all types of murder, all grave bodily harm, and other mis -- maltreatment of a person. This falls within the same category, and in the war crime against civilians or wounded persons or prisoners of war have the same elements. The victim is a person, and this is why this -- they have the same characteristics in terms of perpetration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Assaults against another person of any type, they would be within this category, would they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I ask those questions because I notice that the maximum sentences that seem to have been imposed are only in two cases and in the range of two to five years. The sentences, most of them, were in the range one to two years. They could hardly be killings, could they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was most probably for mistreatment or grave bodily harm. Later on we have information on convictions for murders. This is a view dated as at the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sorry, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, let's continue where we left off. You explained to us the punishment for criminal -- grave or more serious criminal offences in the penal code of the Republic of Serbia, but in the penal code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia there was a crime against civilians. What article governed that, how -- what was the definition of that criminal offence, and what was the punishment envisaged by law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be war crime against civilians which is Article 142, and it says, Whoever orders, concerning military officers, saying, whoever orders contrary to the principles of international humanitarian law for civilians to be murdered shall be responsible and those who perpetrated the act and the punishment envisaged is 15 or 20 years. When the capital punishment was abolished, this alternative sentence of 20 years was introduced in the federal law. So if it's not 15 years, then the other possible punishment is 20 years, not 16, 17, or 18, but either 15 or 20 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And bearing in mind what we discussed yesterday in terms of criminal proceedings pursuant to the Criminal Procedure Act, it is at the discretion of the prosecutor whether to prosecute under Article 42 of the Serbian penal code or Article 142 of the penal code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. What was your experience in terms of which options the military prosecutors took in such cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, prosecutors tend to use the more serious qualifications for the simple reason that that leaves them room for manoeuvre to adjust downwards. If they start out with more lenient qualification with the same body of proof, they cannot then pre-qualify that upwards. This is how the law is stated and this is why they used the more serious qualifications from the outset. And then later on such grave offences were tried by military courts later on. And at courts, the courts re-qualified those criminal offences as war crimes and -- because it was more in favour for the perpetrators of criminal offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Just a brief explanation concerning the question that you received from the Bench. In your experience, investigation procedure and trials for criminal offences against life and limb, primarily murder, aggregated murder, crimes against civilians, how long did investigations take and how long trials took?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were complex criminal offences because of the method of perpetration, and proceedings lasted longer than in the case of other criminal offences because they needed or required expert witnesses, expert analysis, because particularly where -- in cases where organs of detection and investigation and prosecutors did not arrive at the crime scene until much later when -- which then involved disinterment, excavations, analysis, forensic work, which means that this took a long time. It could not be done while the state of war prevailed in Kosovo. But as soon as the state of war no longer was in force, such cases were handed over to civilian courts, which then continued those proceedings. And this is why in the tables we will not have many completed cases because the military courts had temporal limitation of their jurisdiction over those.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now to finish with this topic, but bearing in mind what we said yesterday. First of all, this table on the 15th of May, 1999, we see the last day that was taken into account. But could you tell us what was the first day for which this data pertained?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This data are from the beginning of the work of the courts until the 15th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So was it on the -- did they start on the 24th of March, 1999, when the state of war was declared?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, one cannot take it literally. Yes, the courts were established on the 24th and the 25th of March, and the cases started trickling down only somewhat later, after 15 or 20 days. So the day they were established they did not have case files on their tables, on their desks. Just taking into account that there were preliminary steps that needed to be taken before the case was ready for trial. So formally speaking the table pertains to the crimes between the 24th of March and the 15th of May, so the offences carried out within that period of time. Now as for the cases when they started arriving at the desks of prosecutors and judges, it was somewhat later, after the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, to go back to this table - and again bearing in mind what we said yesterday - we see here that where it says "category of persons," it says "soldiers," and then "crimes against life and limb," we see that there are certain figures there. Tell us, please, how long did investigation and trials normally last for such grave offences if this involved soldiers who were no longer soldiers, who had lost the status of a military personnel and the indictment was not issued during that period of time, what happened to such cases?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday we spoke about subject matter jurisdiction of military courts, namely that they had jurisdiction to try certain perpetrators of crimes. The majority of the personnel in any unit were conscripts who were serving their regular military service plus those who had been mobilised. Once they stop being military person, once they leave a unit, and if they were perpetrators of a crime, the case would be sent to the competent civilian court if they no longer were soldiers. The majority of the cases had this fate, especially complex and grave crimes, in cases where the person was no longer in the military, regardless of whether that person was a private or an officer or a non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the following page of this document, both in B/C/S and in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So we see a document entitled: "List of Accused per Category of Person and Type of Crime on 15 May 1999." General, are you familiar with this list, who drafted it, and just very briefly explain the figures.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This list accompanied the earlier document that we analysed just now, and you will see that the figures in the previous document and the previous table and then in this table are consistent with each other. You see also the indictees here, the accused persons, because lists and tables were made for those who were sentenced and for those who were accused. So we can see here that the number of indictments was greater than the number of cases that actually reached the courts. And the methodology is the same. It was categorised based on crimes and based on perpetrators, be it officers, non-commissioned officers, privates, civilians in the army, civilians not in the army, and so on. So this is an overview, based on which one can assess what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see page D011-1267 in B/C/S and D011-1273 in English. Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So what I'm interested in this document is the last page and the figures that we can see on the last page. You told us that this document was a document accompanying the information dated the 12th of May that we saw just now. Could you please briefly comment on these figures, and are they completely identical as those that we saw in item 3 of the document dated the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a summary overview of the entire table that shows figures pursuant to the court data. First we had a general overview, then we had a table categorising courts and armies, and then this one. And all the figures are consistent, both in the tables and in the information dated the 12th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, did you draft such tables in peacetime? Was there any need to draft such tables in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In peacetime military courts and prosecutors were not duty-bound to make reports and similar overviews other than once a year. Normally after the year was over, they would draft an annual report on the work of military courts. That is to say, each military court and each military prosecutor had to draft such annual reports. As for military -- as for supreme military court and supreme prosecutor, they would compile those reports and produce their own annual report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So the drafting of these overviews and tables, was it a reflection of the fact that there was insistence on knowing what was going on in the military judicial system and that it followed certain orders and instructions?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These reports that the courts and legal administration drafted on the work of military courts was not aimed at finding out what the courts were doing, but rather for the commands of units to know what was the situation with regard to the crime in their units so that they could take appropriate measures. So this was just an X-ray of the crime situation in units. Based on these analysis, commands would produce their own analyses and then send it further to units with instructions to undertake measures to prevent, mostly prevent, commission of crimes and also to forward any information to prosecutor and courts. So this was primarily intended for unit commands in order for them to act preventively so that there would be no crimes committed. Once this was done, it was too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00507.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D011-1286.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Which is tab 16 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To make it easier for my learned friends, that's 953 on the Prosecutor's 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we see information on the work of military judicial organs during the state of war from -- it was dated 21st of June, 1999. Are you familiar with this document? Do you know who drafted it?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could we also see the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with this report. I drafted it. You can see at the bottom my initials, and this is the final information or final report after the state of war was over. It is a summarised report, using the same methodology to present data on the situation with respect to crimes committed in the military, categorising all types of crimes, listing the number of criminal reports filed, number of investigations sentenced in the first instance, sentenced in the second instance, on-site investigations conducted by investigating judges, and percentage with respect to crimes, from which chapter how many crimes were committed so that you can see an overview of the types of crimes committed. And then sentences, implementation of sentences, and so on. At the end is a brief assessment of the work completed. So the volume of information was large, and it had to be summarised in order to produce this report, and this report also included tables with figures so the methodology was the same. The types of crimes were listed, types of -- categories of perpetrators, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Just a question concerning this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the paragraph beginning with the words "according to the types of crimes perpetrators of the crime of failure to respond to a call-up and evasion of military service under Article 214 ... were the most numerous accounting for around 70 per cent. Around 18 per cent were perpetrators of the crime of wilful abandonment and desertion of the army under Article 217 ... the remaining 12 per cent were perpetrators of other crimes."

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So it is immediately obvious that the largest percentage of perpetrators committed crimes under Articles 214 and 217 of the Criminal Code, but the remaining 12 per cent committed other crimes. Was this figure arrived at on the basis of criminal reports filed?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to arrive at these percentages they used the number of criminal reports filed. Whenever something is shown in percentages, then the same basis is used for calculating the percentage. So these 12 per cent, just like in previous cases, was calculated on the basis of 18.540 criminal reports filed. So we can see that the greatest number of perpetrators committed a crime of failure to respond to the call-up, and so on. This is a very large number, but bearing in mind that between 40.000 and -- 400.000 and 500.000 conscripts were mobilised, then you can see that these percentages are not very illustrative. They can be tricky to analyse.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So 12 per cent out of 18.541 criminal reports are those who perpetrated other crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct, other crimes that do not fall under Article 214 and 217 of the Criminal Code.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I tender this document into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00508.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see D011-1299.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Which is your tab 17, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for my learned friends from the Prosecution, I think that's 954 from the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, we see here a letter from the military court in Nis dated the 20th of August, 2001. It was sent to the supreme military court in Belgrade. Are you familiar with this document? What are its contents, and why was it drafted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with this document. This is a document that was sent by the military court in Nis to the military court in Belgrade at its request. The purpose of this report was, given that already at that time the prosecutor of ICTY had demanded certain information from Yugoslavia on commission of crimes that fall in the area of international humanitarian law, the supreme military court found it necessary to obtain that information since all of the cases processed by the courts during the war that are related to the 3rd Army fell under the jurisdiction of the military courts in Nis during wartime. So all of these criminal cases after the state of war was declared over, the courts and prosecutors were duty-bound to hand-over their cases to peacetime courts. So all of those courts who had jurisdiction over the 3rd Army transferred their cases to the military courts in Nis. The military courts in Nis conducted analysis of these cases and drafted this report showing only those criminal offences which fall under the category of violations of international humanitarian law, which is to say all kinds of murder, crimes against property, sexual abuse, and so on. So this covers only those crimes which in their view could have been a violation of international humanitarian law. And this document lists information based on the chronological order of reports and minutes. And this is authentic documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In order to speed up the proceedings, I'm just going to ask you if this document is the basis for you to draft another document; and if yes, can you please tell us exactly what it is about.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to remind the Trial Chamber that at the time I was the deputy of the chairman of the commission for co-operation with The Hague Tribunal, and this document was sent to the commission or to the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, and on the basis of this review I drafted another overview. And because it's treated here in a chronological order, it wasn't really classified, it was done in the order that the cases came to us, I made another overview where I sorted all the crimes according to the categories and made a much more acceptable and understandable overview which is authentic and tallies with these -- this information here from the court in Nis.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask the Trial Chamber to admit this document and then I would like to move to the next document that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00509.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have Defence document D011-1451.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And this is tab 18, General, in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for my colleagues from the Prosecution, this is 65 ter 955. Your Honours and my friends from the Prosecution, I'm going to read the title, and this is the only document actually -- actually, the only page of this document that is not translated. And the title of the document is: "An Overview of Initiated Criminal Proceedings Against Perpetrators of Crimes in the Kosovo and Metohija Area During the NATO aggression from the 24th of March to the 10th of June, 1999." This is the only page that was untranslated. The rest of the document is translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And this is why I'm going to ask you, Mr. Gojovic, whether this is the document that you drafted and where you chronologically treated all that was provided in the previous document to the General Staff. Now you took all that information and put it together in categories for the purposes of this commission?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I did in order to provide a logical overview and that anyone who has the overview in their hands would be able to follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, while you were preparing for this testimony did you have the opportunity to look at this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You told me then that you wanted to make certain corrections in the document, so I would like to ask to see page T0 -- D011-1454, and this is in the B/C/S version and D100-1523 [as interpreted] in the English version. Yes, that's the page. We see a summary review of criminal proceedings instigated against persons who committed crimes in the area of Kosovo and Metohija during the NATO aggression from the 24th of March to the 10th of June, 1999. Sir, could you please tell us what are exactly the corrections that you wanted to make to this document?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be precise, there was a typing error here. The table was done on a regular typewriter and not on a computer, so it was very difficult to correct it once it was all over. In the case talking about aggravated theft and robbery with loss of life, in the column talking about the number of victims, the information was not entered from another table where the number of victims is stated, and that is number 6. So that in relation to these crimes we need to add the actual number of victims here in this column which is empty, this is column 6, because later from this authentic table you can see that these perpetrators committed six killings -- they committed the crime of killing six civilians in one house. And this is in the column for serious cases, grave instances of robbery and violence to --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: So just to be precise for the English version, this is the crime from Article 169, and this is the fourth box from the bottom. And then the first column from the top where it says "number of victims," so in this box that corresponds to this grave incidents of robbery and violence to retain stolen goods with murder, Article 169, paragraph 2, the number 6 should be as the number of victims. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw this immediately. I didn't want to add this by hand. I left it as it was, so I did immediately indicate that error. Later in this crime grave incidents, crimes against civilians, four people were sentenced after that, after this summary report was written, so then number of victims in this column corresponding to that box we need to add two -- I'm going to repeat for the sake of the interpreters. In this case in the column of war crimes against the civilian population, for this crime, four persons were charged and sentenced for this act. So the victims were two civilians. So in the vertical number of victims where the number of victims is eight, we need to add two more victims, which would then make the total ten for this particular crime. And then in the very last column where it says "total," so next to that -- in that particular box we need to add four more victims. And then this crime, war crimes against civilians, this is on the next -- on the following page, we need to add the names of those four perpetrators of those crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We will do that definitely. I would just like to make one more correction. I think you didn't mention it. In the first column where the number of victims is cited, if you add two for war crimes against the civilian population and six for grave robberies and theft with loss of life and then we have the number 37, in that case we would have 45 people?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be the logical thing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page D011. This is 1456 in the B/C/S version and D011-1526 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We see that this is an overview of the war crimes against civilians from Article 142, paragraph 1, of the penal code of the FRY. You spoke about those four persons that would need to be added to the figures here.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are the four persons that would need to be added to this overview.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read the names and you can tell me whether those are the persons involved.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember, the case involved a major. His name was Zlatan Mancic, then Captain First Class Rade Radojevic, military conscript Danilo Tesic, and Seregi Misel.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, now that we're talking about these four perpetrators of crimes, do you have information about the course of these proceedings; and if you do, do you know what sentences were passed on these perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can remember, they were tried before the lower military court in Nis. It was competent to try this particular case because this was a military personnel subject to military courts. This other person too was an active military officer. As far as I can remember, this first one was sentenced to seven years' imprisonment, the second one to five years' imprisonment, and the military conscript was sentenced to four years' imprisonment, and the last one, Misel, was sentenced to three years, if I'm not mistaken. Then the prosecutor appealed and the supreme military court passed down significantly higher sentences. The first one was sentenced to 14 years, the second one to seven years, five, and four years of imprisonment. I think that is what I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know later what happened to these cases. I really don't know what the final outcome was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, before I asked for this document to be tendered into evidence, I would like to ask for us to look at a case which I would also later ask to be tendered. I wanted to show it to the General. It actually is an integral part of these tables and overviews that the General drafted. So can we please look at D011-1604.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is number 19 in your binder. We can see tables which are identical to the tables that we saw in the previous documents, but the heading on this one is, "Rape," Article 103, paragraph 1 and 2 of the penal code of the Republic of Serbia. And then we have the names and last names of the perpetrators with a brief description of the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at the following page.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We can see now this is an overview of cases of "Attempted Rape," Article 103, paragraph 1, in conjunction with Article 19. Can we now look at the following page in both versions. Once again, "Attempted Rape," Article 103, paragraphs 1 and 2. General, my question to you is this: These two overviews that we have seen in this document, are they an integral part of the previous document which is a larger document? Are they part of the overview that you made because these pages are marked with the numbers 14, 15, and 16. This is how the documents were read into e-court, separately, and I'm just asking you in order to be able to follow a certain logic later when we use the document again in the course of this case.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This overview is an integral part of the previous overview, and it was part of the whole document. It was in chronological order, pages 14, 15, and 16, so I'm surprised that it was taken out of the chronological order and is being treated separately. I had arranged the crimes according to their gravity, and that is how I dealt with them. So this is an excerpt from pages 14 to 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. For the reasons we have just heard I'm going to propose that the last two exhibits, if possible, be tendered as one document in view of the fact that this second document actually is an integral part of the previous document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Popovic. Before they are received, the Chamber was not able readily to follow the amendments and additions suggested by the witness. The Chamber would like to explore how it would be possible to get an amended, corrected version of the original table either by yourself and counsel for the Prosecution looking at a prepared amendment and being content that it reflects what was set out in the transcript by the witness. If that doesn't prove possible, is there some other means that occurs to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think we will easily resolve this issue in the manner that you proposed because those amendments followed from the fact that the General, who had authored this document, compared and noticed when producing the document this discrepancy and found out that not all the figures that should have been introduced there were introduced. I'm sure that I will be able to do so with my learned friend, and as Defence counsel I will pin-point to my learned colleagues the crimes, perpetrators -- the perpetrators and the victims not included in the summary overview and the table derived from it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we'll do then is to receive as one exhibit these two documents in e-court, and we would authorise there to be added to the exhibit the amended, complete version. And we would ask that if there is any difficulty in preparing that amended, complete version, that that be raised again with us in the course of next week. So it ought by the end of next week be the position that there is an amended, completed version incorporated into the exhibit in e-court. Is that a clear enough indication?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber will receive the two documents as one exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00510.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm about to broach another topic here on the basis of a new document, so I do believe that it would be a fitting moment to adjourn for the break. And during the second session I believe that Defence will very quickly finish its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I'm heartened to hear that, Mr. Popovic. We notice that both with this witness and the last witness two hours was allowed in the schedule. We've been more in the category of two days for the first witness and over a day for this. Thank you. We will now adjourn and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Before the witness enters the courtroom, during the break I took the opportunity to try to find the simplest way to resolve the problem with the document as instructed by the Bench, and I did it with my learned friends from the OTP. I believe that we found the appropriate way. I'm going to go back to that document and ask the witness to pin-point the page of the document that was omitted from the table, to make the appropriate markings, and to try to overcome that problem with the table as existing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think we can express a view. We don't quite understand the document yet nor what you have proposed, but we have trust in you, Mr. Popovic, so we will look forward to this exercise producing a solution for us. We want a document we can follow at the end of the exercise.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. This is exactly what we were trying to do. Let's re-visit the previous document, that would be Exhibit D510. The page is D011-1464 in the B/C/S version or D011-1536 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, we discussed the table and amendments that you introduced into the previous document, that would be tab 18 in your binder, and you said that there were certain corrections, that is, that there's been an omission with respect to the number of victims of the crime of aggravated theft with violence resulting in death from the one -- from Article 169, paragraph 2, of the penal code of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. To make matters clear to the Bench and the OTP, could you please tell me whether the page that you see on the screen is what you discussed and whether in the box, brief description of the criminal offence, does it contain the number of the victims that were affected by those crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it lists the names and surnames of the victims. There's no need for me to read them. And when we add them all up, the total is six. And that piece of information is not introduced into the summary table in the appropriate line. This figure is not shown there, and this is the amendment that should logically follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: To make matters even clearer, let's go back to page 1454 in the B/C/S version and page 1523 in the English version, and see that in the fourth row from the bottom in the English version which makes mention of Article 169 and the criminal offences perpetrated and that would be grave instances of robbery with violence resulting in death, there is an empty box, and you just indicated the page which bears records about six victims. So this is the discrepancy between this table and the information in the summary?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in the content of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thanks very much, General, sir. I hope that we've managed up to a point to clarify the situation with respect to the amendments to the summary overview that should be effected. If the Bench believe and my learned friend from the OTP, that additional amendments should be made to make matters perfectly clear, the Defence is willing to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we hope to achieve, Mr. Popovic, is a document which fully and correctly sets out what the witness' table sought to achieve; in other words, a document which includes and incorporates the amendments and changes which he has spoken about orally today. If that can be achieved, we would be grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, yes. Absolutely, yes. And we will make sure that in the shortest possible time the new summary overview is delivered to the Bench with all the amendments that the witness testified about and a new table mentioning war crimes against civilians with the amendment containing the names of the perpetrators as testified about today. I hope that we'll be able to do so and deliver to the Bench and to the OTP next week such amended documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now let's take a look at D217.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That would be tab 20, General. General, sir -- well, let's wait for the English version to appear on the screen. Thank you. This is an order by the Supreme Command Staff dated the 10th of May, 1999. The question for you is whether you know about this document and who drafted it.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm familiar with this document. I personally authored it, and I initialled at the last page. And the chief of the Supreme Command Staff signed this document, but it bears my initials.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Let's go briefly through this document. Let's continue -- let's start with paragraph 1, saying -- I apologise. So it reads: "All commanders, unit commanders, and other superior officers must undertake all (necessary) measures in their units to ensure that every individual unit member adheres to the principles, rules, and regulations of the international laws of war when conducting combat operations and beyond combat operations." Could you please comment paragraph 1 of this document, and what are the reasons to draft such a document on the 10th of May, 1999.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason for drafting this document was that by the time when it was authored on the basis of criminal offences that had occurred until that time, the need arose to highlight that issue once again and to address such a document to all unit commanders and superior commanders and to remind them of their obligations under international humanitarian law. And obligation was introduced into the defence act, and I tried to adapt this to the circumstances to make it unequivocal, clear, and binding to all commanding officers, which of course by law they were bound to do anyway. But this is an instance where the most superior command was instructed them and ordering them to be mindful of these obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's go to paragraph 4. It reads: "Any military officer who knows that there have been violations of the principles, rules, and regulations of international laws of war have been perpetrated and who does not initiate disciplinary or criminal proceedings and such military officer shall be held personally responsible." General, sir, is this another insistence on detecting -- preventing, detecting, and sanctioning violations of international humanitarian law?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's it exactly. In all legal systems the most difficult bit is to detect and identify both criminal offence and the perpetrator, because perpetrators try to destroy any traces or evidence of the criminal offence they perpetrated. And this is why we emphasize the personal responsibility of anybody who learned about such criminal offences and failed to report them. And the emphasis here is on military officers. This was another way to pressurise them to control their subordinates. This is the only way that you can undertake appropriate and effective measures down on the ground so that such occurrences do not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's turn the page on -- in both versions and take a look at -- and let's take a look at paragraph 6. Paragraph 6 reads: "Go through the annex to this order regarding criminal liability for war crimes and other serious violations of international laws of war and crimes against humanity and international law with all members of Yugoslav Army commands, staffs, units, and institutions." First of all, I'm going to ask you this: Who are the addressees of this order of Supreme Command Staff, who are the recipients?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order was delivered to all commands that are subordinated directly to the Chief of Staff Supreme Command. That would be commands of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd Army, as listed here, command of the air force and anti-aircraft defence, the navy command, establishment units which are immediately connected to the Supreme Command Staff, command of the 72nd Special Brigade, to the Guards Brigade, and to the 46th Motorised Protection Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please explain to us this wording "with all members of Yugoslav Army command, staffs, units, and institutions," how was this order forwarded further on? How did all the others learn about it? What was the way that it was presented to them?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appropriate way of distributing and disseminating orders emanated from the General Staff of the Supreme Command Staff is for that order to be sent to the immediately subordinated commands, and then those in the list of addressees must prepare their own orders on the basis of this order, which may not be more restrictive than this one. It can be -- their orders can be only more expanded versions or more detailed versions, and they have to deliver those to their subordinated commands. So this order is supposed to percolate down to all levels of units, down to company commanders, which would be the lowest level obliged to disseminate this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 6 that we read, in the second sentence "go through the annex to this order." Was there an annex to this order? That's my question to you.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an annex to this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This exhibit has already been admitted, but when it was admitted the annex was not admitted, which is an integral part of this decision. So I would like us to look at D011-16112, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1612, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And this is in tab 22 in your binder, sir. The document is entitled: "Annex Regarding Criminal Liability For War Crimes and Other Serious Violations of the International Laws of War and Crimes Against Humanity and International Law." Sir, is this a document that was an integral part of the order of the Supreme Command Staff of the order of the 10th of May, 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the annex to this order, and I felt that it was important to attach the text of the law pertaining to those particular crimes so that those who were reviewing the document would be able to see the gravity of those crimes. So it was not sufficient just to abide by the order, but also to be aware of these crimes which were specified in the law and to be aware of the sentences that each of those crimes carried for each perpetrator so that all the units would have the appropriate attitude when encountering such occurrences.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell us briefly what the subtitles of the annex are. Can we just briefly go through each of the items, and then we can move to the next document.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The headings are those of the particular crimes that we're dealing with, for example, the war crime of genocide, war crime against the civilian population, war crime against wounded and ill persons, war crimes against prisoners of war, then violations -- grave violations of the rules and regulations of war - and they are specified, and finally which are the crimes that are classified according to the law. And this is for the purposes of informing in detail all the people in the units and commands so that they would be able to adequately and seriously conduct themselves during combat and not only in combat but generally in war, not only when they were in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to ask, since the document is an integral part of D212 -- 217, that it be then added to document D217. So for those two documents to be admitted together because that is the annex to that original order, if this is agreeable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This document will be added to and incorporated as part of Exhibit D217.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now we're going to be looking at the last document. This will be document D006-0333.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In your binder this is in tab 21. This is a summary report on the work of military judicial organs and the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia's legal administration during the war. It's dated the 6th of September, 1999, and the signature is by Chief Colonel Radomir Gojovic. Mr. Gojovic, it's quite superfluous for me to ask whether you are the author of this document, and that is why I'm going to ask you this. In the cover letter the first sentence states: "On the basis of the received remarks ..." Can you please explain what this was about and then we can get into more detailed discussion of the document.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal administration was obliged, just like any other organisational unit of the General Staff and the other units, to draft a report about the overall work of each of its organisational units or the legal administration during the state of war. And this material was then placed into -- it was actually then compiled into one file which represented a study of that overall period during the war in order that certain conclusions could be drawn to it -- from it. So this report then was submitted to the section, and they had some remarks as to the methodology of the report because they had some certain guide-lines about what each of these analysis should contain. So then they gave some remarks to certain elements, how they needed to be covered. So then this report was then compiled in accordance with that methodology the document was compiled, and it was placed in the General Staff archives which General Staff then used in order to deal with the issue of the work and operation of military tribunals and courts during the state of war. It was used for general analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The document contains a lot of information that was already covered and we talked about in previous reports, so this is why I'm not going to dwell on that particular aspect of the document. Can we look at page D006-0336 or 0357 in the English version, the previous page referred to the B/C/S version. The fifth section -- actually in paragraph section 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters would kindly ask to look at this paragraph on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is this in some way the conclusion on the work of the military judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is the conclusion because we needed to show here as much as possible in an objective way the situation that we had found ourselves in and the war -- military courts were put into operation for the first time since the end of World War II in the -- because since then there had been no war on the territory of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, so now the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was in war with the forces of the NATO Pact.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It seems --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And terrorist actions in Kosovo and for the first time pursuant to the criteria as soon as the state of war is declared pursuant to the constitution, then all the potential of the state for defence of independence, autonomy, and territorial integrity are placed into operation including the judicial organs or, rather, military courts are being formed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I see that the interpreters have asked to have the part of the text that I read on the screen so that it could be in the transcript. General, so you already answered that question. There is no need for you to repeat your answer. The sentence that I read is the fifth paragraph in order in section 4, "osposobljenost," and it says: "In spite of these shortcomings and the fact that this was the first time that military judicial organs were mobilised in wartime, they were organised and equipped to function in a state of war relatively fast." This is paragraph 3 on the page we are currently looking at. Yes, I think that's what it is. In any case, thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please look at section 8, and this would be page 0339 in the B/C/S or 0360 in the English version. Yes, that's the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We were talking about the independence of the military judicial organs, and it seems to be a precondition for the military courts to function in the proper way. In this particular section, section (d), subheading "with regard to working conditions," in the second paragraph it says: "Some commands interfered unacceptably in the work of courts and the adoption of decisions by making requests concerning the type and length of sentences that should be pronounced by courts ..." and then in parenthesis "(one order even instructed the court about the length of sentences - the command of the Novi Sad Corps). "By undertaking measures mentioned in earlier items on time, the problems were resolved, and all judicial organs entirely fulfilled their legally defined functions ..." First of all, I would like to ask you to comment on this, even though you mentioned yesterday in your testimony something that refers to what is said in the paragraph that I have just read, how such situations were resolved and how the independence of military courts was preserved during the state of war.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could be precise here without any dilemmas military courts are completely independent in the -- in their decisions. Everyone knows that, and they are quite capable of using properly this independence of theirs. There was this quite ridiculous incident when the Novi Sad Corps issued this order. One senior officer who had submitted the criminal reports in the cover letter instructed that this should be punished in the strictest possible manner and proposed the sentences. When the prosecutor and the court received this, they reacted immediately, not in the sense that they would succumb to that; no, there was no question of that. But just as an occurrence they immediately informed the supreme prosecutor and the president of the supreme military court --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, very well. And this president of the court, this judge, we know each other because we used to work together, he called me on the telephone and then he mentioned: Oh, can you imagine what is happening and mention that this would -- that we would need to put a stop to that. So he reacted immediately and then when attention was drawn to this, to that particular senior officer, he apologised. He didn't really think that it was such a serious matter, what he wrote in that cover letter regarding expressing his opinion in terms of the sentence. There was another such case from a person who had submitted the criminal report. So this sort of went together with that, and this incident actually drew our attention to the occurrence so that we could put it in the analysis and through training and study and review of this material we would be able to train the senior officers that in no circumstances whatsoever, including a situation of war, should they express their own opinion as to any kind of work of the court. So this was one incident that happened, and it was with great pleasure actually that I included it in my analysis in order to be able to draw attention to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to look at the last page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And I am going to ask you, General, to look at the last paragraph on the last page of this document, and I would like to ask you --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid that this is not the right document. The page is D006-0341 in the B/C/S. In English it's D006-0362. Yes, that's the correct page. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: General, can you please read out the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On page 8?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. It begins with the word "however."

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is one of the final conclusions from the analysis and states: "However, due to timely measures undertaken by the legal administration of the VJ General Staff, adequate assignments, the expansion of the wartime manning table and reorganisation of some courts, as well as the issuing of various orders, instructions, and manuals, the above-mentioned difficulties were gradually remedied. This allowed military judicial organs, despite the initial and subsequent difficulties in their work in complex conditions, to carry out fully and very successfully with maximum engagement and effort, all of their tasks and to fulfil their functions as defined by the constitution and law" --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you then, on the basis of this, draw a general conclusion as to the situation in the forces during the state of war?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly it. First of all, we had to pin-point certain problems at the early stages, those who prepared manning tables and the establishment had not been right in their assessments in terms of the complexity of the tasks at hand. This was identified and such problems were removed in mid-stride, and all the conditions were created in very short period of time, in two months. Quite a lot of effort and energy was invested into that, and the appropriate results were gained within the remit of the -- that justice system.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By this we conclude our examination-in-chief of this witness, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic. Are you wanting to tender this summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems to have been put into e-court along with a number of other documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is an integral -- well, integral parts of this document are also some other documents, summary report on the work of the legal administration of the General Staff of the VJ, but since the witness authored the document and confirmed that, and since I did not have a need to go through all those other overviews because he testified that this was just a summary of what had already been published in earlier reports that we had occasion to see in the previous documents, I just wanted to highlight what was important in those documents, and I would like to move for this document to be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You would like this one document out of that batch to become an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That will take a little time to achieve, but I'm sure we will manage it --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting you. I believe that the whole document with the annexes can be admitted because they are an integral part of the report that we discussed, I and the witness. I explained the reason why I did not go through the whole report, to save time, and because of the fact that we've already heard quite a lot of testimony about that previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will receive the document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00511.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And before we move on, perhaps you could assist me in one further matter. At a number of points in your evidence you have referred to the General Staff and at others to the Supreme Command Staff. It may be a matter of English translation, but are you seeing those as two distinct bodies or as different names for the one body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
