utterances.text: [Interpretation] It goes two labels for the one and the same thing. The General Staff is an institution that heads the army in peacetime, and pursuant to the Yugoslav Army Act, it functions under the same label in wartime as well. From earlier times there was this wording Staff of the Supreme Command or Supreme Command Staff. It had circulated from earlier times dating back to the times of the SFRY, while Comrade Tito was the supreme commander. But later on it was renamed General Staff. It goes for the same level of command but different names are used depending on which document you're reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gojovic. I have some questions for you today about your testimony over the last two days. You've had a chance to review a number of documents that you have prepared, and I'd like to begin with some questions about these documents. Let's start with the last document that was tendered, which was D511.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If we could call that up on e-court, please. And could we please go to page 6, heading 8 in the English and the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the correct section to be called up on e-court, Mr. Gojovic, as I understand it this document updates an earlier document that you prepared, and this is D508, which gives similar conclusions. And I will take you to the relevant section in a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page of the English, please, and I'd like the same page in the e-court for the B/C/S, and that's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like you to look at the paragraph beginning: "By type of criminal act the largest number of perpetrators committed the criminal act of failure to respond to call-up ..." Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So in this document that you prepared in September 1999, the percentage of perpetrators relating to violations of Article 214 is 70 per cent and another 18 per cent related to violations of Article 217; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And that gives us a total of 88 per cent of perpetrators for offences relating to the VJ?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And the remaining 12 per cent, perpetrators of other criminal acts, that would be perpetrators of criminal acts such as crimes against life and limb, which you described earlier; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and all the other criminal offences, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And to confirm, this report updates your earlier report of July -- of June 1999, which provides the same figures; so this is the final version?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The June version was the final version, but it provides the basis for this report, this analysis. If you allow me, may I point out that the only figure which is higher here than in the previous one is the one which is amended by the prosecutor. It says here 19708 some new criminal reports had been received, other figures are identical. So there is this discrepancy, 19.000 in this one and 18.000 in the previous report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And aside from this discrepancy, you would agree with me that in terms of percentages of the figures that we just went through, the reports are identical?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'd like to call up 65 ter 1182.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, a document will be appearing on your screen shortly, and this is a report on criminal proceedings before military courts of the command of the PrK, and it's dated the 15th of May, 1999. And I have some questions for you about the types of offences listed in this document. It's not a document that is in your binder, I don't think so; it's a document that's appearing on the screen. Do you see it there, Information on the situation and movement of criminals among professional military personnel?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose document is this?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: If you go to the top of the page, it is a document prepared by the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like you to just have a glance through the types of offences listed in this document. For example, paragraph 1 refers to violations of Article 217, and that's the article that we just saw in the previous two documents; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page in both languages, and if you scroll through the different headings. For example, paragraph 2 refers to the crime of theft; paragraph 3, the crime of aggravated robbery. Are you able to follow?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes. And paragraph 4, crime of failing or refusing to obey orders; 5, crime of seizing vehicles; 6, crime of abuse of position; 7, embezzlement; 8, failure to fulfil duties; 9, unauthorised departure; and 10, failing to take steps to protect the combat unit. And I'll let you scroll down the rest which are in the following page, number 11 to 23 onwards. Now, if you look through these various headings and the numbers, that is, the names of the perpetrators listed under these different headings, you will find that there's only one reference to the crime of murder, and that is in item 20. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: From the information here, the other cases listed mainly concern crimes against the VJ, for example, desertion, refusal to obey orders, and a limited number of cases concerning theft and robbery. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So the information in this document is consistent with the information you provided in the earlier two documents that we saw, to the extent that a large number of the crimes that were prosecuted by the military courts related to crimes committed against the VJ, for example, desertion, failing to obey orders; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that I expressed are based on the information received by the court. The information reported by the corps command is based on the criminal reports that they filed. Each criminal report -- it's not necessarily that every criminal report has been accepted by the military prosecutor. So it's logical that a large number of such criminal offences being more easily detectable are the most numerous and are subject to criminal reports. More serious criminal offences are more difficult to detect because the perpetrators try to be furtive about it, destroy evidence, et cetera. But this number of criminal reports does not necessarily correspond to the number of indictments and criminal proceedings, but this expresses the obligation of the corps command. They have to press charges or send criminal reports, and it is up to the military prosecutor to decide whether to prosecute or not, of course, and for all those --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, if I may just clarify your point. So based on what you're saying, these are reports that were provided up to the courts. Now, it appears to me based on this information here that a large number of the reports related to crimes committed against the VJ, for example, desertion, failure to obey orders. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01520.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to take you to another document that you were involved in, Mr. Gojovic, and that is D510, and this is the overview of initiated criminal proceedings. I believe that's tab 18 in your binder. And if we could go to the summary table which is on page 2 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S. Now, just to remind ourselves, Mr. Gojovic, this report was prepared when you were the deputy chairman of the commission of co-operation with the -- with this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And when was this report prepared?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2001, because when the authentic report was received from the courts, it was drafted on the basis of those preceding documents. We have a date of it being received. Let me just find it. The supreme military court received it on the 21st of August, 2001, and this would be the 8th of May, 2003 -- well, this one was drafted in 2001, sometime in 2001.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could have a look at some of these figures in the table. I know that you have made some corrections, and I will incorporate those into my questions. Now, what we see here is a summary of the criminal proceedings in Kosovo and Metohija during the period of the war, is that correct, in the military courts?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This overview provides only criminal offences and perpetrators which could be covered under the heading "Violations of International Humanitarian Law," only those, not the other ones. And this shows only that portion.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's start with the first heading on the first column, which is, "War Crimes Against Civilians." So sometime in 2001 the figure for the number of victims of war crimes against civilians is eight, is that correct, that's what the table says?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, but that's only the period while military -- wartime military courts were in place and worked, and there were some amendments that we just did in this courtroom which in 2001 saw judgements. So that would be the 24th of March to the 10th of June, 1999. This pertains only to that period. But later detections and proceedings are not included in this table. There was a number of such proceedings, but I did not have any obligations with respect to that so I did not include that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll come to the later proceedings in a moment, but for now in terms of the information that was available in 2001 we see that there were eight victims of war crimes against civilians?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's only the -- row for these criminal offences, but there are 46 as the total number of victims, where victims were civilians but victims of different criminal offences. There are other criminal offences resulting in death, which means that we have to add up to 48 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, I'm sorry to interrupt you, but I will come to the rest of the offences in a moment. At present, I just want to confirm the numbers of victims for war crimes against civilians. And based on the table before us, I believe that's eight.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Eight, yes, that's not contentious.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And how about the number of cases that were referred to another court, also for war crimes, is -- does that still remain at the number six?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that figure remained at the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to look at the columns relating to murder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could I interrupt to ask, does that mean that of the eight cases in which criminal proceedings were instituted in the military courts, six were transferred to the civil courts; or does it mean that there were 14 cases all together, eight in the military courts and six in the civil courts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This must be another misunderstanding. The first column indicates the number of victims, the result of criminal offences. Six persons are prosecuted under the column case referred to the jurisdiction of another court, meaning the competent civilian court which held jurisdiction. Therefore, during the state of war proceedings were instituted against six persons for war crimes against civilians. They were not finished before military courts, but during the investigation stage they were deferred to another court. That's the number of cases, and the number of victims is in the first column.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sorry for interrupting, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, in this table we see that there -- in 2001 there were no judgements issued for war crimes against civilians. I see that the column for judgement is blank, but you mentioned during the course of your testimony today that there was a judgement given; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was handed down later on in 2002 or 2003. I'm not sure, handed down by the military court. There were judgements by civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in terms of the sentences for this judgement - and I think we're referring to the Misel case, you mentioned the figure of 14 years, but that was not the final sentence; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And we see here under the columns for murder that there were no judgements given in 2001. Are you aware of any subsequent judgements?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could in your questions refer to the following -- well, this is the state of affairs at the 20th of June, 1999. This is when wartime military courts ceased operating, and this is the overview as at that date. Let's not deal with 2001 to avoid confusion, but otherwise this figure is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: As I understand it, this document was prepared in 2001?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The document was drafted in 2001 based on the information related to this particular time-period. We did not draft a report relating to other periods.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So following the end of the war, did you have any information on judgements relating to murder?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the end of the war, peacetime military courts took over all the other cases, but where perpetrators lost the status of a member of the military they were tried by civilian courts, not military courts. And we did not collect information from the civilian courts because military organs do not have this method of communicating with civilian courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojovic. We'll come back to that in a moment. Now, before we leave this document, I just wanted to confirm the figure that you gave for the total number of victims. I believe there's been an increase in the figure, and you gave -- did you give the figure of 46 as the total number of victims?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we have additional six persons, so 37 plus eight is 45.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, another question I have about this document relates to involuntary manslaughter. We see there -- and that's the seventh column from the top. We see there that three judgements were issued for involuntary manslaughter by June 1999; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And now in your report, this is the summary page, but the rest of the report contains further details of these crimes. And I'd like to take you to the section on involuntary manslaughter which is on pages 14 to 15 of the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14 and 15 is not included here. That would be the excerpt on the rapes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: In that case, perhaps you could have a look at the screen, Mr. Gojovic, and we could have the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll find it here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: It should be the full section, not the section relating to rapes. And it's numbered page 14 at the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have it here, I don't have it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I can help, 14, 15, and 16 in the B/C/S version were admitted, these are rapes and attempted rapes, so that the pages 11, 12, and 13 in the B/C/S version are probably what my learned friend is actually trying to discuss. 14 is rape, and we can see that on the screen. So 11, 12, and 13 would be probably the corresponding pages in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages 11, 12, and 13 are missing in the review -- overview.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the pages on the screen, Mr. Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: They are different pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yeah. I will resolve this issue in terms of the page numbering and come back to this section.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I am told that pages 11, 12, and 13 are not part of the e-court document for some reason. So we have, apparently, an incomplete document in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Perhaps I could show these pages to Mr. Gojovic and request that it's tendered as the remaining portion of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. But before we pass from it, may I ask Mr. Popovic, is it the case then that we don't have this complete document as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're absolutely correct, Your Honour. From what I see, pages 11, 12, and 13 of the document are missing, but we can very easily resolve this. I don't know if the witness has the original document with him, which would contain all those pages, so if Madam Gopalan would like to use the pages in English, he could use his document and follow from there. I think it was probably some kind of error when the document was being uploaded into e-court. I didn't pay attention to those pages. I didn't really need them for my examination-in-chief, so I didn't pay attention. Probably that's how the error occurred.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I ask you to verify that we have a complete exhibit, and if necessary authority is given for any omitted pages to be added so that the exhibit is complete. Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, in the binder that you have, are you able to locate these sections relating to involuntary manslaughter? No?

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Well, if Mr. Gojovic doesn't --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me explain. I don't have the document with me. I have my original at the hotel, where these pages do exist. I notice that these pages are not here, but this information in the review is correct. The pages are missing. I do have those pages in the document, the complete document, at my hotel, the manuscript. I could provide that to the Defence later, and then you can use that to complete the document. If an explanation is necessary, I can give an explanation what the Prosecutor is asking --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, I suggest what we do is to wait for the correct pages to be uploaded on to e-court during the break, and I will pick up this issue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, although it's not clear to me that the missing pages are readily available. Are they available to you, Mr. Popovic? They appear to be at the hotel, whichever hotel that is, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: We can also -- yes, we can also check our records, Your Honours, because the 65 ter number was a Prosecution exhibit. So we may well have the relevant pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will continue. The position is not satisfactory. We will do what we can to get back into complete order.

utterances.text: So we found the English, which is page 56. Yes, that is the one. And we want the corresponding page in B/C/S. Is that page available in the B/C/S? It's the section headed "Report 9" if that's any help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The court staff are having to go through the whole document page by page in an attempt to find what it is you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. Perhaps there was an issue with the uploading because I had checked the e-court pages for the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What we will do is take the second break a little early -- you have a number, Mr. Popovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. If we're talking about Slobodan Stosic, that is page D011-1343 in the B/C/S. I think that's the correct page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And I think that it's page 45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now your questions, Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: We see here Slobodan Stosic who is a lieutenant-colonel. He is being charged -- this is in the third column, Article 142. Am I correct that that is the Article relating to war crimes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And there are a number of names listed below Mr. Stosic. I believe these were his subordinates who were involved in the killing of the five Albanians that is listed in the third column; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, if we go to the second-last column relating to this case, we see that proceedings against Stosic were discontinued and -- let's begin with Stosic's proceedings. Do you know why they were discontinued?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain. The proceedings were not adjourned. They were discontinued, they were stayed. When one adjourns or discontinues, you can always continue with it, meaning that the case is not continue -- is not completed. But in this case it was stayed, and it was not re-instituted again because it was established that Stosic was not the perpetrator of a crime but the others who were charged in order to place themselves in a better position said that they had received an order for him and then they took the people out and did what they did. And in order to justify their actions, they said that they had been issued this order by Stosic. This is why the prosecutor did not prosecute Stosic and the others were prosecuted, and I think that then this case was completed under the jurisdiction of the civilian court. So that this initial information is not as it actually was. Stosic is not in the data that I included, because by that time already the proceedings against him were stayed. But the others of course were subject to criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, when you mentioned the data that you prepared and Stosic not being included in that, could you give us more detail on the type of crime his subordinates were charged with. I believe the document you just referred to contains further details.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have a brief summary here. I can read it, if you permit me.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says: "Oto Palinkas, Miodrag Miskovic, Bozidar Sudarski, Dragan Milosavljevic, killed five persons of Albanian ethnicity, whose identity was not established. They were previously captured in an action by the unit and detained. After being taken out of detention they were brought and placed in front of a wall of our house where automatic fire was opened from weapons. They were killed and thrown into a well where petrol was then poured and set on fire." This is a brief description of this particular crime and when it was established that they were responsible they said that they were told to do this by Lieutenant-Colonel Stosic. Proceedings were instigated against him, and then later it was established that he did not issue such an order to them but that they did this of their own accord. And later it was established that this particular group committed several similar crimes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, speaking of these several similar crimes, could we go to P964, please, which is a Prosecution exhibit. Now, we see here that this is a report of the supreme military prosecutor, and it's dated the 9th of April, 2002. And paragraph 1 relates to the Stosic case. And as you mentioned, there are a number of different cases that involve this lieutenant-colonel. The first incident is the one that we spoke about just now that you mentioned. Now, you also see in the preceding pages that this group was also involved in other criminal activities, and the details are there. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had the opportunity to look at this report by the supreme military prosecutor. It's based on the same data that was available to me, and basically from what I could see, it was always this group Oto Palinkos, Bozidar Sudarski, whereby they committed some crimes and always in their defence they attempted to imply or state that this was done as a consequence of Stosic's suggestions. I guess they were in his unit so they would mention him. As far as I'm concerned -- as far as I remember, in this period that I analysed, no further proceedings were conducted against Stosic, and I think on the basis of this we can also see that there were some proceedings conducted against him and then it was established that he actually was not involved in these events.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, if we add up the number of victims mentioned here in these three different incidences, we get the figure of around 28 victims, six in the first paragraph, two in the second, and another 20 in the third paragraph. Now, it would seem that although Stosic was suspected to have been involved in the killings of this number of civilians, no proceedings were taken to the completion with him due to lack of evidence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is legal term, insufficient evidence, because if you were to say that there was sufficient evidence there would be grounds to suspect that he was involved. However, there is no evidence at all of his involvement. It was only the perpetrators who did actually commit mass crimes, serial mass crimes, asserted that, and it would have been easy for them to place the blame on their superior officer. I don't know Stosic, but I think a man would have to be crazy to issue such an order. No officer in his right -- in a right state of mind would issue such an order. The fact is, though, that all of this was happening with members of his unit. So he also had to be included in the investigation to determine what was it that he knew and because it was his duty to prevent it what steps he took. Had the prosecutor had any evidence, he would probably have initiated proceedings against him, but he -- I mean, he would have no reason not to proceed if there was enough evidence pointing to Stosic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the proceedings against Stosic's subordinates, do you know?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I know is that they were convicted and later the -- the sentence was quashed on appeal, and then I don't know what happened. The first-instance proceedings, they were sentenced to quite severe sentences; and then the Supreme Court of Serbia quashed the case, and it was returned for re-trial. I don't know what happened. It was not really part of my duties to follow what happened with that particular case later.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I believe it's time for our break now, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the second break and resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. Gopalan.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic, during your testimony yesterday, you provided a clarification on the obligation on the part of a citizen to report a crime, and this is in page 10330 of the transcript. Now, you referred to a federal law provision, and you said that: "An official person which learns ex officio that a criminal offence has been committed punishable by five years in prison or more and fails to do so, then they may be punished by three years in prison and more." What I'm interested in is the types of offences that would fall within this federal law provision. Would murder be included?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The law would include murder. The law dealt with crimes that were subject to sentences of five years of imprisonment or more. It was up to the official to report such a crime. If the crime was not reported by a senior officer, they, themselves, would then be subject to a sentence of up to three years' imprisonment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Would looting be included?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Murder, looting, subject to a sentence of five years or more are all included in that particular law.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: How about burning of civilian property?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serious punishment or sentences are also envisioned for such crimes. Burning of property during wartime would be a type of war crime because it would be inflicting harm on the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, you were also asked some questions about the obligation to report on the part of a VJ officer, and I'd like to ask you about this obligation to report when the MUP officer sees a crime being committed -- I'd like to rephrase the question -- when the VJ officer sees a crime being committed by the MUP. Now, based on your answers yesterday, the obligation arises that the VJ officer reports this crime to the appropriate authorities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. An officer is obliged to report, just like any other citizen, and in particular because of his function as an official to report any crime. In practice and based on our experiences from these cases, the bulk or majority of the cases, 80 per cent of them, were reported by military officers, not just for simple crimes, but also murders. We have a lot of cases that were initiated against unidentified persons. The victims of those crime number up to 600. Most of these crimes were reported by military officers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, just coming back to your answer on crimes that were covered by the war crimes provision, what would the crime of expelling someone from their home fall under, which provision would it be covered under?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Expulsion's quite a narrow term, expulsion from one's house or home, it's covered by Article 122. It includes also being expelled from one's state, one's country, not only transfer from one location to another that would be affected by war. This -- both of these crimes would constitute a crime against the civilian population pursuant to Article 142.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, in the schedule that you prepared for us which set out the list of cases that were processed under Article 142, that was D510, how many cases were listed for expulsion? And while you're looking at that, I'd just like to clarify whether you were actually referring to Article 122 in the transcript. Is that a separate article you had in mind, or has it been incorrectly recorded?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't want to speculate on exactly which article of the law that was. I could make a mistake, but the gist of it is that it would be a crime from this set of laws against -- on crimes against international humanitarian law. Article 142 is quite substantial and lengthy, and it would encompass expulsion, as you refer to it, displacement of the population from their place of residence and their expulsion from their country of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, concerning what my learned friend tried to correct, this whole and entire answer does not correspond to what the witness said in the Serbian language. I may accept that I'm about to address this in my re-direct, but to clarify the whole thing, I would like my learned friend to ask this question again so that the answer would be properly put into transcript. Because what we read in the transcript does not correspond with what the witness said in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I leave it to you, Ms. Gopalan, whether you wish to go back over that or move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: I'm satisfied with the answer, Your Honours. I'll leave it to my learned colleague to deal with it later if he chooses to.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, in response to my question on the number of expulsions that were listed in the schedule that you prepared, how many are contained in the schedule?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These criminal offences which were subject to proceedings and from the description of the criminal offence which the prosecutor prosecuted do not include the act of expulsion because the prosecutor found that there was no intention to expel them across the border because it is impossible pursuant to effective laws of Yugoslavia to expel one's own citizens. This would be legally unacceptable formulation, and it's true that some segments of the population of all ethnic background in Kosovo and Metohija left their places of residence because of combat activity. This is a relatively small area with quite substantial military effect on both sides. And naturally, the civilian population moved away from such fighting.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojovic. I'll now move on to another document, and this is 65 ter 845. If we could go to the second page of the document. Mr. Gojovic, are you able to see this document on your screen?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it, although it's poorly legible, but I know what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And if we scroll down to the bottom of the page, I believe -- and the next page in the English, I believe this is a document that you sent?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And you sent it in your capacity of being the deputy chairman of the commission for co-operation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And we can see here that this document relates to charges of rape and sexual assaults in 1998 and 1999. And going through this document we see that, just focusing on 1999, that there were a total of seven perpetrators who were involved in proceedings related to rape and sexual assault?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And that is the sum total for the period of 1999?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the period of 1999 this is shown in this overview in the descriptive part and in the summary overview, and these are -- this information from the previously discussed materials and documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And do you know how many of these related to proceedings during just the period of the war, so ending on the 10th of June, 1999, and not going beyond that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This refers exclusively to that period, during the state of war. It doesn't include information preceding that period or subsequent to that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P01521.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Going back to a document we were looking at before the break, that's D510, and this is the summary that you prepared, the overview. Hopefully we've got the right reference pages this time. If we could go to page 7 of both the English and the B/C/S. And I'd like to ask you some questions about the case of Petrovic. Now, we see here on this table that Dragisa Petrovic was a major. Have you found the relevant page, Mr. Gojovic?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you must have told me the wrong page number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Could you have a look on the screen perhaps.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be page 4 in my binder. I found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. And you see there it's a page headed "Murder, Multiple, Article 47, paragraph 2," and so on. Yes?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, there's some detail here in relation to the crime itself, but I'd just like to confirm that Article 47 is part of the Serbian Criminal Code; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, the detailed description of the crime is that Petrovic ordered three individuals to liquidate Feriz and Rukija Krasniqi, an elderly man and woman who had not left the village, and they did this by shooting with their automatic rifles. Now in your earlier testimony you provided further information, and you testified that the woman who was shot was bedridden. Is that correct? That information is not contained in the summary, but it just provides further detail to the nature of the crime.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a summary. This is not a detailed description. This is the briefest possible summary because of this very small box, but in the indictment and in the judgement you could find more detailed description. This was not necessarily here in this box. I also indicated that such situations did occur. There was such an incident, possibly the one that you mentioned, but there's nothing disputable about this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. And these were two elderly people, and you testified about this incident in the Milutinovic testimony. And do you recall that the convictions for these murders were nine years for the major and seven years for the subordinates?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. These are the sentences handed down in the first-instance proceedings. I cannot tell you because I don't know what happened later. I know that the first-instance judgement was as you just mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And in the first-instance judgement, this was the sentence for the murder of two elderly people, one of whom was bedridden; correct?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. As I said, this was not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd now move on to another section in this report, and that's page 65 on the B/C/S and page 73 of the English.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Can you repeat the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: It is the e-court page 65 on the B/C/S, and I will give you the paper -- page in a moment. I believe it's page 68 of your binder. Sorry, the B/C/S is 65 on e-court and 68 in the witness' binder.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: And is the English page 73? Now, while the document is being called up, you'll see here that this refers -- item 1 refers to an incident near the village of Izbica, and it says here that an investigation was initiated on the 29th of May, 1999. And this incident was classified as a murder. Could you tell us why it was classified as a murder?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the initial information, it concerns 144 grave-sites, freshly dug graves of persons unknown. This is the information that the military prosecutor received from a military officer of a unit from Krusevac on the 29th of May, 1999, and he registered it under this criminal offence because it's qualified as severe case of murder under the Republic of Serbia penal code, which envisages more severe punishment including the death penalty, which was still valid for the republican law. And I discussed this circumstance where the prosecutor was duty-bound by law to include in his draft version the most severe qualification of a criminal offence, and this is why he took the appropriate action and qualified this criminal offence as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gojovic, let me just stop you there. You mentioned that the crime was qualified or classified as a murder because that envisages a more severe punishment, which is the death penalty. Could you tell us when this extreme or the more severe punishment was applied, if at all? When was the last time it was applied?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was applied very rarely. As far as I can remember between 1980 and 1985 was the last capital punishment carried out, in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: So you would agree with me that in 1999, considering the death penalty to be a punishment was just a theoretical possibility?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only a theoretical, but also practical. However, the jurisprudence was such that the courts almost never opted for that because pursuant to the federal law capital punishment was abolished. And the FRY's penal code was adjusted to the European Convention abolishing death penalty in most countries. Those countries which retained death penalties were considered as retrograde. The republican penal code maintained that capital punishment, but the federal law was amended to abide by European Conventions. And criminal offences against international humanitarian law were governed by federal penal code, which did not envisage capital punishment --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojovic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- at the time the republican penal code did still envisage that, but it has been amended in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, there's mention here about a request made for gathering intelligence in relation to this Izbica incident. Could you tell us what the outcome was of this investigation?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pursuant to the Criminal Procedure Act, if the perpetrator of a crime or perpetrators, most probably perpetrators in this case, if they're unknown, then the prosecutor has an option --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Mr. Gojovic --

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- to continue collecting all --

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: -- I apologise for having to interrupt you, but unfortunately we're somewhat short on time. So perhaps I can rephrase my question so you're able to answer more briefly. What I would like to know is the outcome of this investigation. Were criminal proceedings initiated? For example, was there ever a judgement issued in relation to the Izbica incident? That's what I'm interested in: What was the outcome?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These proceedings are not completed. It's within the jurisdiction of the district prosecutor and the war crimes prosecutor. It's still pending. It hasn't been brought to trial, and they're trying to identify the perpetrators, but it's within the remit now of the district attorney or district prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Gojovic, we've had evidence in this case that the remains of some of the bodies found in Izbica were later found in mass graves in Petrovo Selo in Serbia proper. Did you know that -- do you know that?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From which site? I did not understand this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: The bodies that were found in Izbica, the Izbica site, so the incident that we're talking about now.

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I do not know anything about that because I did not follow the situation. Later on I heard it and read in the press that personal identification documents were found somewhere else, but it wasn't very intelligible to me because pursuant to all the information here, the graves were marked and those remains were interred pursuant to rules of the International Committee of the Red Cross and other legal provisions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojovic. Now, you are someone who has a lot of experience working in the army and the military judicial system. You may not be aware of the precise circumstances in which the remains were found in mass graves later on, but let me ask you this: If bodies or remains of bodies from Izbica were found in mass graves elsewhere, you would agree with me, won't you, that no proper investigation was conducted into this massacre in the first place?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, some investigation was done of the mortal remains. Disinterment was attempted, autopsies carried out, but what happened later on I don't know. It's possible that -- that may have happened, but it's unacceptable from any aspect, both criminal law aspects or other aspects. I don't know what the reasons were after the detection of such crime for the remains to be relocated. I don't know who -- what guided those who relocated them because it has -- serves no practical purposes. The criminal offence had been registered, procedures been initiated. There's no rational explanation for moving those mortal remains.

utterances.speaker: MS. GOPALAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Gojovic. I have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gopalan. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Gojovic, when we talk about the summary overview of the initiated criminal proceedings against perpetrators of crimes that we had occasion to see and where you stated together with the amendments that there were 45 victims, are we talking about perpetrators of criminal offences which -- who are named, known, whose residence is known and who became subject to criminal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the summary overview and in the tables, those refer to victims, crimes, and perpetrators, where we know the name and surname of the perpetrator and what he/she is charged with, and the consequences of such criminal offence and the victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's take a look at D510. That would be page 011-1514 in B/C/S and 011-1552 -- 92 in the English version. Thank you. General, sir, that would be page 67. Summary review of persons unknown who committed multiple murders, Article 47, paragraph 2, item 6, of the penal code of the Republic of Serbia in the area of KiM during the NATO aggression in Yugoslavia from March 24th to June 10th, 1999. Is this a summary review of perpetrators unknown, and is the number of victims 598?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's summary review of crimes committed by unknown perpetrators. Criminal proceedings are conducted against persons unknown. There were 11 cases, 598 victims, maybe an additional three victims should -- are recorded somewhere else. So this is the conservative figure, the lowest possible figure, of 598 victims.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we are hard-pressed for time my question would be: Concerning all those 598 victims, was the proper legal procedure conducted?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for all those cases the military prosecutor initiated proceedings either directly through organs of detection and investigation or through investigating judges. Five cases were deferred to competent public prosecutor, five have been subject to gathering of intelligence reports. These statute of limitations for these crimes do not expire.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What about the Izbica case, was the investigating judge -- did he do his part?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, pursuant to law within his duties. The crime scene investigation was conducted there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, asked by my learned colleague on expulsion from home. What would that criminal offence be? Your answer -- in the case of your answer, the transcript does not correspond to what you said in Serbian. So I'm asking you again. Expulsion from home, what kind of a criminal offence would that be, and what is envisaged by Article 140?

utterances.speaker: RADOMIR GOJOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Expulsion from home does not constitute a criminal offence except for arrogant behaviour. It is not sanctioned by law. But what the Prosecutor's question is hinting at is expulsion from the territory of the country, and this is what was aimed at. At the local level there was displacement of persons, people moved away from conflict and combat areas, and this is something which is envisaged by rules and laws anyway, to move them from harm.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions in my re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You'll be pleased to know, sir, that that concludes the questioning for you. The Chamber would like to thank you for your attendance here in The Hague and for the assistance you've been able to give us in looking at this range of matters, particularly as many of the legal aspects are not ones with which we normally deal. We thank you. You may of course return to your normal activities and a court officer will assist you from the court. This seems a very convenient time, Mr. Popovic. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
